newsitem.title: JAPAN: NEC entry heats up race in rewritable memory discs.
newsitem.headline: NEC entry heats up race in rewritable memory discs.

text.p: Japanese computer giant NEC Corp said on Thursday it would launch its own high-capacity rewritable data storage disc in 1998, casting another challenge at the flagging global standard for a next-generation medium for video, audio and computer data.

The NEC move follows closely on the heels of Wednesday's announcement by Sony Corp and two other electronics firms that they would also pursue their own standard for rewritable digital video discs (DVDs), abandoning a common format unveiled just four months ago by Sony and nine other DVD developers.
NEC's entry is certain to intensify format competition in rewritable memory discs, for which three different groups had already proposed separate, incompatible formats.
DVDs, with far greater storage capacity than conventional video cassettes, CDs and CD-ROMs, are already available with read-only memory (ROM).
But a dearth of video titles and other pre-recorded content available in the DVD-ROM format, combined with the inability to record films or other material, has limited their popularity.

Industry officials hope that rewritable discs, such as the DVD-RAM (random-access memory) disc agreed upon as a common format by 10 manufacturers in April, will boost the new technology's popularity. The first DVD-RAM products are expected to reach the market by the end of the year.

Competition among DVD-RAM and the formats adopted by the Sony group and NEC, however, could slow acceptance of the new technology by consumers, many of whom will be reluctant to buy DVD-compatible PCs before a clear standard is established.
Yet another group, a 15-firm consortium led by Fujitsu Ltd , has also said it would bring to the market magneto-optical discs of about six to seven gigabytes by the end of 1998.

NEC said its proprietary rewritable disc, called multimedia video file (MMVF), will have greater capacity than both DVD-RAM discs and the rewritable disc announced on Wednesday by Sony, Philips Electronics NVand Hewlett-Packard Co .
"DVD-RAM discs can record only one-hour of moving pictures. Users will find this limited capacity a problem when they try to record two-hour films," an NEC spokesman said.

NEC's MMVF format will be able to hold 5.2 gigabytes of information, or two-hours of motion pictures, on a single side, double the 2.6 gigabit capacity of DVD-RAMs and considerably larger than the Sony group's 3.0 gigabits.

The MMVF will not be compatible with DVD-RAMs and users of MMVF-installed personal computers will not able to read or process data and pictures recorded on DVD-RAMs, although they will be able to read DVD-ROM discs currently in use, the spokesman said.
Sony said its rewritable discs would also be compatible with DVD-ROM, but not with DVD-RAM.
Analysts said NEC is in an advantageous position in the disc format race because of its large market share in personal computers.
NEC holds a 40 percent share in Japan's domestic PC market and about a 10 percent share in the global market, including sales of its affiliate Packard Bell.
The NEC spokesman said the company has not decided yet whether it will start selling MMVF-installed PCs next year.
Among the four competing groups, DVD-RAMs, supported by such companies as Toshiba Corp , Matsushita Electric Industrial Co and Hitachi Ltd , will hit the market at the end of this year.
Sony said its group has not yet decided on the timing of the launch of its products.
